Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China 's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.
Chinese tech giant Alibaba , which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.
The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.
As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.
Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”
“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.
“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.
A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.
Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.
“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

MANAMA, Bahrain — Conferences in the Persian Gulf are usually positive affairs, with government officials, executives of state-owned companies and armies of consultants touting petro-fueled visions promising fantastical technology and prosperity.
Yet optimism seemed in short supply at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security and geopolitical summit held in the Bahraini capital. Instead, the dominant mood among the Middle East diplomats, defense officials and experts assembled last weekend was fear over the consequences of another bout of U.S.-Iran fighting.
“The rules of logic tell us that the Iranian stand and the American stand are far apart. And if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” Anwar Gargash, a presidential advisor in the United Arab Emirates, said in an address at the summit.
Gargash added that it’s not in the interest of the regional countries or Iran to go through another round of war.
“While we’re going through this period of protracted crisis of no war, no peace, we are clearly seeking a political offramp,” he said.
In his address, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said, “We have to push very hard in order to prevent the escalation.”
Noting that more fighting would affect food and energy security, he added, “The second round will be more dangerous, more destructive and it will lead to nowhere.”
The signals from Washington are mixed.
With a settlement between Tehran and Washington seemingly out of reach, President Trump has hinted he could launch “another little Operation Epic Fury” after Tuesday’s midterm elections. He was referring to the U.S.-Israeli operation that launched the war on Iran on Feb. 28.
But on Monday, he wrote on his social media website that “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!”
Still, hours later, Iranian state media reported explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz; the Associated Press quoted an unnamed U.S. official as saying the military had carried out “defensive strikes.”
The news comes as Republicans face a tough midterm race, which has become a referendum on an increasingly unpopular war that could sink Trump’s Teflon-like electoral appeal.
Iran has expanded its threats but says it is awaiting the latest U.S. response. The latest proposal Iran has publicly discussed would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping within two days if Washington meets several conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political life after an inconclusive election last month, is said to be pressing Trump to finish off the Islamic Republic.
Behind the scenes, regional diplomats are engaging in furious shuttle diplomacy to avert renewed fighting. Last week, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials flew to Tehran and met with Iranian military officials. Qatar is leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, with Tehran presenting  a de-escalation plan that has yet to be accepted by Trump.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Monday told the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency that it was now up to the Americans to decide “whether they have the will to take the wise path of diplomacy or, as in the past, seek to drag the situation into aggression and military operations.”
“If they dare to test us again,” he added, “they know that they will receive a much more bitter and severe result than before.”
His words came as several Middle Eastern countries are still reeling from the first round of fighting, when Iran retaliated against U.S. attacks by striking American military bases on regional soil with fusillades of drones, as well as cruise and ballistic missiles.
Iran also targeted civilian infrastructure and has vowed to exercise less restraint and wage a no-holds-barred campaign — possibly striking energy, desalination and travel facilities — in the event of a new assault.
On Saturday, Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said further U.S. attacks would prompt a broad response, one without “geographic limits.”
The scars of the fight could be seen around the Bahraini capital, where the U.S. 5th Fleet has several support facilities. Structures showed signs of explosive damage, including a partially destroyed radar dish and soot-covered depot, a result of Iranian projectiles — 500 drones and roughly 200 ballistic missiles — finding their mark.
The bases seemed all but abandoned, with word among residents that American service members, a common sight in Bahrain, have all but disappeared.
The war has cast a shadow on Persian Gulf nations that have long presented themselves as paragons of stability in a volatile region, mostly unaffected by the conflicts raging in the wider Middle East.
Disruptions to energy flows and logistics mean members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, or GCC, a bloc of oil-rich Gulf nations, are facing a 4.8% contraction in gross domestic product compared with last year, according to the International Monetary Fund.
The International Monetary Fund expected a strong turnaround in 2027 but acknowledged that “uncertainty remains exceptionally high, and risks are firmly tilted to the downside.”
Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are hardest hit; Qatar’s real GDP is down more than 15% this year. Meanwhile, the Saudi economy — which is contending with the double pressures of a sealed-off Strait of Hormuz and a blockade on Red Sea access by Iran-backed Yemeni rebels known as the Houthis, shrank almost 4% in the third quarter compared with last year, according to official figures.
Despite regional efforts to bring about a detente, the general consensus among attendees at the security summit  was that more war is coming. The summit, which is organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies think tank, drew hundreds of participants.
And for both regional and European officials present, there was a deep sense of uncertainty regarding Washington and its commitment to shielding putative allies from attack.
That has forced Gulf nations — long reliant on a U.S. security umbrella — to look for protection beyond Washington. Yet diplomats lamented what they said was a lack of coordination close to home, despite a long-standing GCC mutual defense agreement.
The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis of Yemen have unsettled Saudi Arabia, a kingdom unused to conflicts playing out on home turf.
For example, militaries detecting projectiles in their airspace that were en route to a target country didn’t warn their counterparts, leaving them with less time to deal with incoming attacks. Others have systems that are not linked to the U.S.’s regional radar net.
“A lot of countries you thought you can depend on were not there for you,” Gargash said. “Why did we sign that agreement many years ago only to see that this agreement was not activated when we all needed it?”
Saudi Arabia has sought to marshal alternative allies through a recently signed pact with Turkey and Pakistan, and has asked Egypt for help — a request Cairo said it would honor by engaging in defensive operations on Saudi territory.
But Abdelatty, Egypt’s foreign minister, said the region requires more than new military engagements and should instead “move from the logic of crisis management to the logic of building an order” aimed at stopping confrontations before they start.
“A war can begin with a unilateral decision,” Abdelatty said.
“But no one can unilaterally control its consequences or stop it.”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock begins trading in record $81B raise with $1.5T valuation
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock begins trading in record $81B raise with $1.5T valuation
articles.content_orig:
Retail investors with access to Anthropic's initial public offering who sell the stock quickly after buying could get penalized by their brokerage firm.
Anthropic said in an IPO prospectus that it expected to make shares available to retail investors through various brokerages, including Charles Schwab , Fidelity, Robinhood , SoFi , E-Trade and some of their respective affiliates.
Follow CNBC' s live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debut
These broker-dealers have "anti-flipping" policies meant to discourage investors who purchase IPO shares — including those of Anthropic — from dumping them quickly. Charles Schwab is the only one that doesn't have such a policy in place.
"One purpose is to discourage 'flippers' who are just buying with the hope of making a quick profit," Jay Ritter, director of The IPO Initiative at the University of Florida, said in an email. "Their selling could put downward pressure on the price once trading starts."
Investors who run afoul of anti-flipping rules may be prohibited from accessing future IPOs, perhaps for several months or even more than a year for repeat offenders. In the worst case, the brokerage may bar them from all future IPOs.
These policies apply only to retail investors who place an order with their brokerage firm to buy the Anthropic IPO at its offering price — something many investors don't have access to.
For example, Fidelity customers are eligible to participate in the Anthropic IPO if they have at least $25,000 in certain assets, the firm said . Even then, customers are "evaluated and ranked" based on factors such as account assets to determine who can access limited shares that may be available, it said .
Importantly, anti-flipping policies don't apply to retail investors who access shares later, once Anthropic stock starts trading on a public exchange, Ritter said.
Of the retail brokerage firms listed in Anthropic's prospectus, Charles Schwab appears to be the only one without an explicit anti-flipping policy.
"At this time, Schwab does not apply a flipping restriction to any IPOs unless required by an issuer," Margaret Farrell, a company spokesperson, wrote in an email. "This is subject to change at Schwab's discretion."
She confirmed that an anti-flipping policy doesn't apply to the Anthropic IPO.
Other firms aren't as lenient, however.
Here's how they could penalize IPO flippers.
E-Trade said it "prefers investors hold shares for at least 30 calendar days."
However, its policy doesn't lay out an explicit penalty for failing to do so.
Selling or transferring out of an IPO within 30 days "may affect eligibility to participate in other new issues in the future," according to its policy. "E*TRADE reserves the right to exclude customers from future participation."
Investors who are allocated Anthropic shares and sell within the first 15 calendar days from the start of trading in the secondary market won't be able to participate in future stock IPOs through Fidelity for a defined period of time, it said :
"The first day clients can sell without being labeled a 'flipper' is the 16th calendar day after the IPO trades," Fidelity said.
Robinhood's policy stipulates that selling IPO shares within 30 days of the IPO is considered flipping.
Such investors "may be prevented from participating in IPO access for 60 days," it said.
SoFi said that selling an IPO position within the first 30 calendar days after trading starts "may affect your ability to participate in future IPOs on SoFi."

articles.title_orig: Hours after Trump-Putin talks, Russia hits Ukraine with massive, deadly attack
articles.title_zh: Hours after Trump-Putin talks, Russia hits Ukraine with massive, deadly attack
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders â Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron â were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."
"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying:  "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Several buildings were damaged in the latest Russian attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that â in the absence of any major success on the vast front line â the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

articles.title_orig: Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC
articles.title_zh: Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC
articles.content_orig:
Watch: What did Trump, Xi and Putin get out of their historic meeting?
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced  he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Trump greets 'my friend' Putin ahead of meeting with Xi
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The three presidents spoke behind closed doors at the Kylin Villa, the exclusive resort in Shenzhen
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
Russian 'nuclear briefcase' spotted at APEC summit
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.
"I was encouraged by some of the commitments that came out of the President's meetings in Asia, particularly the recognition that nuclear war must never be fought," Republican Senator John Curtis said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
But Curtis also said he was concerned about Trump's approach to the foreign leaders, adding that "Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends".
"We should not treat them as though they share our values or interests," Curtis, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, added.
"Doing so risks undermining our national security, weakening trust with our allies, and sending the wrong message about where America stands."
Jeanne Shaheen, a ranking Democratic member on the same committee, chose harsher words in her comment.
"President Trump's 'friend' is a murderous war criminal," she wrote on X.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon

We’ve actually been playing GTA 6 for a few weeks and had to keep our mouths shut like true professional crooks. But now the secret is out: GTA 6 is a masterpiece .
Celebrate its arrival with us by reading our live blog covering the big launch. We shared news, analysis, opinions, and everything else you need as you prepare for your own crime spree.

I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. articles.title_zh: Asian Stocks Set to Fall as AI Enthusiasm Fades: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Global equity markets are heading for their longest losing streak in more than three years , amid growing concerns over elevated valuations of artificial intelligence-related companies. The MSCI All Country World Index is down 0.6% and could close lower for a seventh consecutive session, marking its longest losing streak since September 2023. Meanwhile, investors are increasingly turning to safer assets, including US Treasuries.
Asian markets are leading the selloff, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index falling 3.5% , heading for its worst week since March 2020. Taiwan's benchmark index is plunging 6.2%, South Korean equities are down 5.7%, and Japan's Nikkei 225 is declining 4.7%. Emerging-market equities have already lost approximately 20% from their June peaks, reaching levels traditionally associated with the beginning of a bear market.
S&P 500 futures are down 0.5%, while Nasdaq 100 futures are falling approximately 1% to their lowest level since mid-April , after the technology-heavy benchmark closed the previous session at its lowest level since April. European markets are also expected to open under pressure, with futures indicating declines of around 1.5%. The broad selloff reflects deteriorating global risk sentiment.
Anthropic (ANT) shares fell nearly 5% to $92.60 in after-hours trading following yesterday's stock market debut. The decline highlights growing investor concerns about AI company valuations and whether massive investments in artificial intelligence will generate sufficient profits to justify current market valuations.
Gold is falling 2% towards $3,500 per ounce, while Bitcoin has retreated to $61,500. Precious metals and cryptocurrencies, alongside equities, are suffering from a significant shift in market positioning as investors increasingly price in a more hawkish monetary policy outlook globally.
Fed's Austan Goolsbee warned that US inflation remains persistently elevated, with a return to the 2% target far from certain. In his view, price pressures stem not only from higher energy costs and tariffs but also from robust consumer demand, record investment in data centers, and wealth effects associated with the AI boom. The pace of future interest rate adjustments will depend primarily on convincing evidence that inflation is sustainably moving back towards the Fed's target.
Fed's Michael Barr is also maintaining a cautious stance, emphasizing that inflation remains excessively high while financial conditions continue to support economic activity. He believes further monetary policy adjustments are necessary, although the Fed is not seeking to directly restrict investment levels across the economy. Barr also warns that the combination of the AI boom, increased risk appetite, and looser banking regulations could heighten financial stability risks, while artificial intelligence could potentially accelerate deposit outflows during banking crises.
The Nasdaq 100 selloff continues to deepen, with the index declining for a sixth consecutive session and losing approximately 15% from its recent highs. Anthropic's successful stock market debut has failed to deliver a sustained improvement in investor sentiment, as markets increasingly price in the possibility of several additional US interest rate hikes.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 release a 'write-off' for shops, says trader
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 release a 'write-off' for shops, says trader
articles.content_orig:
The owner of an independent game shop has said the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 has been a "write-off" for his business after he only sold five copies.
Richard Tewksbury, who runs Super Game Shack in the Silver Arcade in Leicester, said he had seen "embarrassing" sales of the game because it was only released as a digital download and not on disc.
In June, developer Rockstar Games said physical copies would contain a code for a digital download rather than the more traditional format. The company has been contacted for comment.
Tewksbury said, while he thinks the game is "amazing", the choice to not sell physical copies with discs was "not great" for smaller stores.
The release of the blockbuster came after two delays to its initial launch date in autumn 2025.
In advance of the launch, GTA 6 generated an estimated £1.25bn ($1.65bn) in revenue based on an estimated 17.07m units sold, sales tracker SensorTower said .
However, Tewksbury said sales at local stores had been poor because physical editions contain download codes rather than discs.
"It is possibly the biggest game hype there's ever been - 13 years people have been waiting for this," he said.
"People are super, super, super hungry for this game - so it's already doing crazy numbers already - but that's not translated for us.
"I've only sold four copies on PS5 and one copy on Xbox.
"It's because it's all digital - no one sadly wants to buy a code in a box. We gave it a little go, but they just knocked it dead with making it digital. For game shops, it's a write-off.
"I'm really behind the game - I think it's amazing - but for shops, it's just not great."
GTA 6 is one of the first major games to only be released without a traditional disc version.
However, Tewksbury said the reality for game shops was that this style of release would be the future of the industry.
Many consoles are now without physical disc drives and PlayStation announced in July that its games would no longer be released on discs from January 2028 .
Sony, which owns PlayStation, said the move came "as consumer preferences and the broader entertainment industry continue to shift away from physical discs to digital".
"This is the way it's going to be," Tewksbury said.
"It's a big effect for us because it was such a massive game - everyone wants it.
"A lot of people aren't even aware that you could actually get it as a code in a box in a shop.
"Suddenly everyone's already pre-ordered it months in advance because the download is so large and [they] aren't thinking about us."

articles.title_orig: Russia Hits Three Kyiv Bridges in Overnight Ballistic Attack
articles.title_zh: Russia Hits Three Kyiv Bridges in Overnight Ballistic Attack
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missile strikes damaged Kyiv’s Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and South bridges early Friday, Nov. 20, prompting traffic restrictions as fires broke out across the capital.
Russian ballistic missile strikes damaged three bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv early Friday, Nov. 20, disrupting traffic between the capital’s left and right banks as fires erupted in several districts.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported damage to the Podilskyi and Darnytskyi bridges, while the South Bridge was struck again.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Traffic from the right bank to the left bank was suspended on the Podilskyi Bridge. Authorities were assessing the damage to the Darnytskyi Bridge.
The South Bridge remained partially operational, allowing vehicles traveling only from the left bank to the right bank, with weight limits of 10 tons for ordinary vehicles and 18 tons for public transport.
Klitschko urged residents to avoid unnecessary car travel and called on businesses to introduce remote work where possible.
A series of explosions rocked Kyiv overnight as Ukrainian air defenses responded to the incoming missile threat.
City authorities reported fires and damage in at least three districts: Obolonskyi, Podilskyi and Holosiivskyi.
In Obolonskyi, falling missile debris sparked a fire in a three-story building, while another building caught fire in a nonresidential area of Podilskyi.
In Holosiivskyi, a strike hit the grounds of an infrastructure facility, with preliminary reports indicating that an office building on the premises had caught fire.
The latest strikes followed Russian drone attacks on Kyiv on Thursday, Nov. 19, which killed one person and injured several others.
Thursday’s attacks also damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies and the landmark St. Volodymyr’s Cathedral, as US President Donald Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China.

articles.title_orig: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
articles.title_zh: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
articles.content_orig:
Trump’s state department says it is examining the ICJ judgment while stressing the need to avoid ‘politicisation’ of the body
The US has reacted with caution to the world’s highest court ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while the EU more effusively framed the decision as a “landmark” judgment.
The historic ruling from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The US state department said on Thursday Washington was examining the judgment while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, in particular vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), which it regards as a renegade globalist institution. The ICJ and ICC are separate entities and the administration has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”. It noted the US is the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”. Shortly after the ruling was read, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said his government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attache from the UK and “calling urgently for a UN security council session to discuss the judgment”.
Australia’s foreign minister, Penny Wong, called for those behind the Myanmar military’s grave human rights abuses to face justice.
In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case, which the US has pushed back on, is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
articles.title_zh: Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper hit in Houthi strike on Saudi wealth fund HQ
articles.content_orig:
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund , was struck on Thursday in a Houthi attack in the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-backed Yemeni group.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense said a Houthi attack on a tower in Riyadh’s financial center caused material damage to several floors of the building and nearby buildings, but no injuries were reported , state news agency SPA said. The statement did not identify the tower, but an accompanying photograph published by SPA showed the PIF Tower.
The Houthis said they had targeted Riyadh’s financial center twice on Thursday, first at dawn and again in the evening.
They also said they had attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Khamis Mushait airbase in southern Saudi Arabia and SADAF Petrochemical Company in Jubail in the kingdom’s Eastern Province. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of these attacks.
The kingdom’s foreign ministry said it reserved the right to take “all necessary measures” to defend its sovereignty and protect its citizens and national assets following the Houthi attack.
The strike blew out windows across seven to eight floors of the PIF Tower, bending parts of its metal facade . It was the second time in less than two weeks that a Houthi attack damaged a landmark in Riyadh’s financial district, with state oil company Aramco’s building hit in a November 8 attack.
The King Abdullah Financial District was closed to visitors following the attack.
Three sources familiar with the matter said the building had been struck by an incoming Houthi missile . The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “dealt with a missile threat” launched towards Riyadh and that debris had fallen.
PIF, which stands for the Public Investment Fund, acknowledged receiving a Reuters request for comment. The Houthis issued no immediate statement on the strike.
The Houthis have been firing at Saudi airports and oil infrastructure since Yemen’s frozen civil war reignited in July amid the US-Iran war. On the ground in Yemen, the group has seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government, forcing it to stage a major retreat at the weekend.
Residents of the Saudi capital were awoken by a loud boom in the early hours of Thursday.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defense issued several warnings of potential danger in Riyadh throughout Thursday, including after the attack, before announcing that the threat had passed.
The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi aircraft had carried out airstrikes on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sanaa early on Thursday, without providing further details.
Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the strikes.
The conflict has dealt a blow to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plans to develop and diversify the economy of Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter and a US ally.
The prince met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh on Wednesday, Cooper’s third publicly reported visit to Saudi Arabia since the Yemen conflict resumed.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months , according to two Western officials briefed by the Saudis on the kingdom’s plans. A third ​source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts.
The sources said the Saudis, who replaced the commander of their coalition fighting in Yemen this week, want to see their allies make gains on the ground before they enter any negotiations with the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the situation in Yemen has appeared to favour the Houthis, who have seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast including the strategically vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, and have surrounded the city of Taiz in highlands overlooking the government’s temporary capital Aden.
In the wider war, which began in February when the United States and Israel attacked Iran , there has been no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations mediated by Qatar.
Meanwhile, there has been an uptick in hostilities in the Gulf in recent days, with Iran firing at US allies Bahrain and Kuwait and US airstrikes hitting Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.
Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen’s government to power ​after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

articles.title_orig: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, top commander reveals
articles.title_zh: UK conducting offensive cyber ops against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, top commander reveals
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: China’s AI Firms Are Addicted to Nvidia Chips. Now They Are Facing Withdrawal.
articles.title_zh: China’s AI Firms Are Addicted to Nvidia Chips. Now They Are Facing Withdrawal.
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.
Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.
A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said.
"The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.
On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.
"AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson.
The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.
"It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."
Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales.
The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week.
H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
"In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest."
The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
— Megan Cassella , Daren Fonda and Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
articles.title_zh: Trump tells skeptical Europeans: "Putin wants to end the war"
articles.content_orig:
BERLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump told Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday they could save money as well as lives by ending the war with Russia, according to five European officials who were briefed on the discussion.
In a call from Air Force One on his way home from meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump lamented what he characterized as the waste of billions to provide Ukraine with weapons and cash for a conflict that is killing so many people, according to three of the European officials, who were granted anonymity to describe a private meeting.
Hours after concluding his encounters with the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Trump had one message for the leaders gathered in Berlin: Putin is serious about negotiating a peace deal with Ukraine.
Momentum for a peace deal has grown in recent weeks after a flurry of diplomatic activity and intensive talks in Europe, Russia and the Middle East. Trump’s meeting in China with Xi and Putin alarmed some of Ukraine’s allies and raised fears that the U.S. president could be won over to the Russian argument that Ukraine and its European supporters have prolonged the war, which began with Russia’s 2022 invasion.
Some of the officials familiar with the call described Trump’s tone as strongly critical of Europe’s ongoing support for Kyiv, while others said he was just communicating in his usual forthright style. One person briefed on the call said the president had merely emphasized how much all countries could save if the war ended and Europe no longer had to pay for aid to Ukraine.
A U.S. official briefed on the call said any suggestion that Trump had told leaders to stop funding Ukraine was “not accurate.” The president was making his long-held view clear that he “wants to bring this conflict to a close,” the official said.
A White House official rejected characterizations of the call as critical of Europeans, saying: “President Trump called into the Coalition of the Willing meeting today and was super upbeat about the prospects for peace and praised the leaders in the room. The President emphasized that the war is extremely costly in terms of human life and financing, and everyone should all be striving for peace because it will save lives and money that can be invested in our countries’ own defenses and prosperity.”
Trump’s argument was that if the war ends, European governments could be spending their money on rebuilding Ukraine or on their own people, the U.S. official said. The president sounded “optimistic” about the prospects for peace and praised the European leaders on the call for their efforts, the official added.
When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting in Berlin whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war.
Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who attended along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, said the U.S. president had “adamantly supported” a peaceful end to this war and this had been his message to Putin and Xi.
“He sent Jared and I here specifically to be a part of the Coalition of the Willing, and he’s given us instructions on doing everything possible to end this war and be supportive of that effort,” Witkoff told reporters in Berlin. “And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with.”
Kushner emphasized that Trump wanted to make a deal with Europe fully involved in the process and had asked the two U.S. envoys to travel to Berlin to “reassure people” about that. The next talks will involve Europe joining Ukraine, Russia and the U.S. at the negotiating table, Kushner said.
He added that Putin is now ready to accept the notion of security guarantees for Ukraine similar to NATO’s Article 5 — a mutual defense pledge by allies to help defend each other if one of them is attacked.
Speaking to reporters later, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was “not sure” all sides had the same understanding of Article 5 as he did. “Because what does it mean, Article 5? That there are some forces of partners on your land. So, my question is: What about American soldiers?” He said Ukraine “would be happy” if the U.S. would put bases in Ukraine “like in the Middle East.”
Germany Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the press conference, however, that Europe is providing funding for Ukrainian defense “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength.”
Merz added: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.”
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Trump’s faith in Putin’s goodwill was “unshakeable” but added that he hoped this time it proved to be well-founded.
“We had a call with President Trump, who was just leaving China,” Tusk said in Berlin after the coalition meeting. “He shared his impressions of his meetings with Presidents Xi and Putin and made some remarks that sounded fairly optimistic, although I have to say they were received in the room with very cautious optimism when it comes to Putin’s and Moscow’s intentions regarding peace talks.”
“But I have to say, I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. I mean, his belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it. But it would be nice, it would be good, if it really turned out, sooner or later, that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”
This article has been updated with additional details. Alex Gangitano contributed to this report from Washington, James Angelos contributed from Berlin and Bartosz Brzeziński contributed from Brussels.

articles.title_orig: Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
US envoy also says he believes Moscow is ‘comfortable’ with a guarantee; Russia attacks Kyiv bridges after Putin vows response for Crimea bridge attack. What we know on day 1,731
US envoy Jared Kushner has said Donald Trump is open to extending Ukraine a security guarantee similar to Nato’s mutual defence clause , but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Kyiv’s allies to “reopen the question” of Ukraine becoming a member of the military alliance. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, told a press conference in Germany: “From America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. We also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.”
Kushner’s comments came after Ukraine’s allies gathered for a summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelenskyy to emphasise support for Kyiv nearly five years since Russia’s 2022 invasion, and to push for a European role in future peace negotiations. Kushner added on Thursday that “we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5 ”. He noted that went with Moscow’s intention to “not have another war” when this conflict was over, while acknowledging “scepticism” over the position.
Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to do the “maximum” to deliver the air defence systems it needed, as well as looking again at Ukraine joining Nato . “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to Nato,” the French president said in Berlin. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Vladimir Putin said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea would be “painful” , after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week. The Russian president claimed he had considered agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed, report Dan Sabbagh and Jakub Krupa .
On Friday, after Putin’s threat, a Russian ballistic missile attack hit three ⁠bridges on Kyiv’s Dnipro River and killed three people , the city’s mayor said, in the ⁠biggest strikes on routes ⁠connecting ​the left and right banks of Ukraine’s capital since the war began. The missiles hit the ⁠ Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges , Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or ⁠traffic restrictions. About ‌15 people were injured, he added. The strikes also caused fires ‌and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people, mayor Igor Terekhov said. In ‌Russian-controlled Luhansk, three ⁠people ​were ⁠killed ⁠in ​a Ukrainian ‌attack, said Russian-installed ‌authorities of ​the ⁠eastern Ukrainian ​region.
The summit of the coalition of the willing on Thursday was co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, Britain and France shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. China, Russia and the US said after their talks they had agreed to a peace statement, but the declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine. The European coalition’s meeting in Berlin expressed indignation at the trilateral’s cosy optics, reports Rebecca Bailey . “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks would “take place soon” , with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the US, Russia and Ukraine. Merz, speaking in Berlin, did not give a date and added that “we are looking for locations on neutral ground”, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location. British prime minister Andy Burnham said: “I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter.”
A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged the historic Saint Volodymyr Cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. “Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day ... At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need,' but analysts warn of volatility
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need,' but analysts warn of volatility
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's blockbuster IPO on Thursday gave markets a much-needed boost after weeks of weakness, though analysts warned that the stock could remain volatile in the coming weeks.
Share of the Claude maker opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 per share, 17% above the IPO price. The offering raised $81.3 billion through the sale of 980 million shares — surpassing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest IPO on record .
Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott described investors as "foaming at the mouth" for the offering, with allocations "impossibly low," underscoring the strength of demand.
"Anthropic's IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment," said Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, adding that markets have been "depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks."
Still, U.S. equities fell sharply on Thursday, with the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to end at 23,879.20, S&P 500 down 2.02% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 2.19%.
Artificial intelligence and technology stocks initially rose thanks to the IPO, but the gains faded as "profit-taking spread across AI-related stocks," said James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers.
While the initial pop was not surprising for such a highly anticipated listing, investors should avoid "chasing the IPO," Walser said.
She expects the stock to come under pressure in the coming weeks as former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang testifies before the U.S. Senate , potentially reviving concerns around the AI sector.
"The shares remain highly volatile," said Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan.
Walser said that any weakness around the time of Huang's testimony could offer an entry point for investors interested in Anthropic, adding that she remains bullish on the OpenAI rival over the long term.
"For investors, it's going to become a blue-chip stock like Google," Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia."
He added that U.S. technology valuations are at ridiculously low levels relative to the "crazy amazing innovation" coming out of California.
Morningstar's Khan struck a more cautious tone, warning investors against getting swept up in the enthusiasm around Anthropic, advising them instead to step back and "carefully" assess the company as a long-term business.
That will depend on Anthropic's ability to scale enterprise adoption, continue improving its models and turn those capabilities into economically useful products and services in the AI ecosystem, he said.
"We remain confident that the firm will be able to execute on all three fronts," Khan added, setting a $92 fair value estimate for the stock.
Walser stated that Anthropic is "extremely important for the overall AI story" as the first non-Chinese large language model developer to go public.
Its listing gives public-market investors their first direct test of how a major standalone AI model developer will be valued and perform outside the chip sector. Meanwhile, rival OpenAI could follow with an IPO sometime in 2027.
"This IPO is the show me moment for the AI story," Walser said, as much of the stock market's AI narrative has so far centered on chipmakers.
